steps: Raise your dominant hand in front of your face in a slightly cupped open handshape, fingers together and softly bent.
Hold the hand at about eye level, a few inches from your face, like a small hand mirror.
Twist your wrist once to turn the hand sideways, as if glancing around to form an impression.
Angle the palm toward yourself at the start of the twist, keeping the cupped shape steady.
Purse your lips and narrow your eyes slightly, as if thinking hard while you size things up.
tip: MIRROR uses the same handshape with a quick double tap and a neutral face; SEEM twists once with a thinking face.

steps: Form an F handshape with each hand, pressing each thumb tip against its index fingertip in a small ring.
Hook the two F hands together by linking the index finger and thumb of one hand through the ring of the other.
Hold the linked hands in front of your torso, near chest height, with the hands close together.
Rock the joined hands gently back and forth twice while keeping both F handshapes intact.
Keep your face neutral and your body still, letting the linked hands show the connection.
tip: The interlocked rings stand for two parties tied together; context decides whether you mean family ties or a relationship.

steps: Hold both hands in front of your torso in loosely clawed shapes, fingers curved with the dominant hand just above the other.
Let the two hands hover near each other, with the upper hand's palm angled slightly downward toward the lower one.
Shift both hands a few inches outward to the sides at the same time.
As the hands move apart, close each hand into a firm S fist, thumb resting over the curled fingers.
Hold a calm, sincere expression, as if resting steady confidence on the other person.
tip: Clawed hands close into S fists as they part — do not confuse it with CONFIDENCE, which uses a different movement.

steps: Hold both hands up in front of your torso with all fingers and thumbs spread loosely apart.
Bring the hands toward each other at chest height until the fingertips of both hands meet in the middle.
Tap the fingertips of both hands together once, as if many people are gathering into one group.
Angle the palms toward each other and slightly downward as the fingertips touch.
Keep a neutral, informative expression instead of the raised-eyebrow look of a question.
tip: All fingers meet for a group session; two index fingers alone would change it to a one-on-one 'meet'.

steps: Form a C handshape with your dominant hand, thumb and fingers curved as if around a camera lens.
Hold the C hand up beside your eye on your dominant side, about temple height.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat and upright in front of your chest, with its palm facing sideways toward the C hand.
Bring the C hand down so its open side lands against the upright non-dominant palm, as if capturing the image.
Keep both palms facing each other sideways during the contact, and keep your face neutral.
tip: This is the take-a-picture sign — context decides whether you mean the photo, the camera, or the craft itself.

steps: Relax both hands into open 5 handshapes, fingers together and slightly loose, with the thumbs ready.
Hold both hands at chest height with the thumbs aimed at your upper chest.
Poke your upper chest twice with both thumb tips, moving the hands forward and back with each poke.
Angle both palms inward toward your body so the thumbs can reach the chest squarely.
Keep your face relaxed and easy, matching the carefree time-off feeling.
tip: One poke usually means time off or spring break, two pokes a holiday; an R-handshape version of this sign means retired.

steps: Form a C handshape with your dominant hand, thumb and fingers curved open.
Hold the C in front of your body at chest height, slightly to your dominant side.
Trace a quick small circle with the C hand, moving clockwise from your own point of view.
Keep the hand upright with the opening of the C facing outward toward your audience as you circle.
Mouth the word 'century' while signing, since viewers usually need the sentence context to catch it.
tip: Some signers shake the C side to side instead of circling; either way, mouthing 'century' is what makes it read clearly.

steps: Hold both hands in loose flat handshapes, fingers together with thumbs resting casually alongside.
Hold the non-dominant hand steady at chest height with its palm facing upward.
Bring the dominant hand down onto the non-dominant palm twice, as if clapping quietly.
Keep the dominant palm facing down and the base hand facing up as the hands meet.
Use a neutral, matter-of-fact expression, keeping most of the motion in the dominant hand.
tip: Same production as SCHOOL — context tells listeners whether you mean a school or the academic sense; it is not the sign for college.

steps: Close your dominant hand into a loose A fist, keeping the thumb sticking up and slightly out.
Rest that fist on the open palm of your flat non-dominant hand, held at about waist height.
Lift both hands upward together a few inches, as if boosting the fist from below.
Keep the non-dominant palm facing up so it visibly supports the raised fist.
Aim the sign toward the person you mean: start near yourself for 'I help you', near them for 'you help me'.
tip: HELP is directional — the lifting motion points at whoever receives the assistance, so no separate ME or YOU sign is needed.
